desk_demand.reading: People search for the problem: 3,770 searches a month name the buyer or the missed-call problem (14,070 with the category terms), up 37.4% over the year. 6 advertisers run 14 active Meta ads on 'ai receptionist', 3 of the 3 rival product pages in the results also run Google ads in the US, and 3 of the top 10 results are rival product pages: money is already being spent to reach these buyers, so the market is real and crowded. Desk research does not decide go or stop; it says the open question is whether buyers pay this business for it, not whether the problem exists.

assumptions.statement: Buyers pay $39 a month on top of their booking plan.
assumptions.evidence_today: None: no one has been asked to pay.

assumptions.statement: Salon and clinic owners lose bookings to missed calls and want it fixed.
assumptions.evidence_today: Support tickets mention missed calls; search demand exists for the problem phrasings.

assumptions.statement: Buyers searching for the problem click an offer for it at a cost the price can carry.
assumptions.evidence_today: CPCs are known; nobody has seen a sign-up rate yet.

assumptions.statement: The AI books correctly on at least 9 calls in 10.
assumptions.evidence_today: The product team has a working prototype on test calls.
assumptions.tested_by: not tested before the build: prototype test by the product team (outside this skill)

assumptions.statement: Existing customers adopt it from inside the app without sales help.
assumptions.tested_by: not tested before the build: in-app fake door after launch

economics.allowed_cac_formula: $39 x 70% gross margin x 12 months payback
economics.allowed_cost_per_signup_formula: $327.60 x 15% of sign-ups expected to pay

sizing.chosen: 90% confidence: 295 paid visits, about $1,858.50 at the planned CPC
sizing.why: At 95% the test needs $2,633.40, over the $2,500.00 budget; at 90% it needs $1,858.50, which fits.
sizing.note: With kill set at half of pass, the test costs about the same whatever the CPC: a cheaper channel lowers the pass rate too, so it needs more visits.

tests.method: conversations with 20 target buyers, no pitch: ask about the last time a call was missed and what they did
tests.metric: buyers who describe missed calls unprompted and have already tried to fix it (paid for a tool or a person, or changed staffing)

tests.method: fake-door waitlist page at /early-access/ai-receptionist/ with a Google Search campaign on the test-set phrasings
tests.metric: waitlist_signup key events / paid sessions to the page (GA4, google / cpc)

tests.method: pre-sale email to every waitlist sign-up: Reserve the add-on: first month at $39, charged now, refunded in full if it does not launch by 2027-01-31
tests.pass: 15.0% or more (6 of 39 once the list size is known)

drafted_campaign.status: not run: shown for confirmation; after the user says yes the campaign, ad group and ad are created PAUSED and the keywords are sent with status PAUSED

keywords.text: ai answering service for medical office

descriptions: Coming soon: an AI receptionist that will answer the calls your front desk misses.
Coming soon for salons and clinics, $39 a month. Join the list to hear first.

readout.detail: 11 described missed calls unprompted and had tried to fix them; 4 described the problem but had done nothing about it. 90% range 37.2% to 71.6% (the conversations were not sized, so 90%).

39 sign-ups from 298 paid sessions (90% range 10.2% to 16.6%), planned sample 295 reached. 309 ad clicks for $1,870.20: actual CPC $6.05 against $6.30 planned, $47.95 per sign-up against $49.14 allowed. At the actual CPC the pass line would be 12.31%, so the result is above it: the economics are as planned. GA4 saw 96.4% of the ad clicks as sessions, so tracking held. Spend stayed inside the $1,876.00 the $67.00 daily budget allows over 28 days. The ad platform counted 37 conversions; the read uses GA4's 39.
Pass needed 6, kill was 2 or fewer. With 39 people the 90% range is 4.7% to 21.0%, so this cannot show yet whether 15% of sign-ups will pay.

decision.rule: go when every must-pass test passes; stop when the riskiest assumption's test fails or two tests fail; change otherwise
decision.why: The problem (T1) and the search smoke test (T2) passed their lines. The riskiest assumption, A3 willingness to pay, landed in between: 4 of 39 paid, under the 6 needed and over the kill line of 2. The search test passed its frozen line and held up at the actual CPC: each sign-up cost $47.95 against $49.14 allowed, so reach is not the problem; payment is.
decision.change: Keep the problem and the channel. Change the offer, not the product: rerun only the pre-sale, with two versions sent to fresh sign-ups (the add-on on its own at the current price, and the add-on included in the Business plan), and pass and kill set the same way before it starts.
decision.do_not: Do not start the build on this evidence, and do not raise the test budget for T2: it already passed.

unknowns: A4 feasibility is the product team's prototype test, not measured here.
The waitlist-to-paying rate of 15% is the user's assumption; T3 is the first evidence on it and is not yet conclusive.
